So, this is sort of an introductory thread and a place to spill mah woes and show off my latest project.

Who knows, maybe someone can help.

My equipment is rudimentary and pretty personal. I suspect that applies to every blacksmith to some degree. My dad and I (he's now passed almost 10 years) made/collected most of it.

My forge is the front wheel hub from a Mercedes Benz cement mixer; I have a few of the stellite leaf springs from the same truck, one of which is a sword that has been sitting around unfinished for most of the time since my dad passed. In fact, all this stuff has been. So anyway. My wife and I bought a house about 25 miles south of Houston just off 45. I decided since I owned the place, I might as well get my smithy up and running and make a few things now and then.

A few trips to Lowes, and I had an anvil stand (I don't have a real anvil, I use a section of forklift fork taken from the back end of the fork), with the 'anvil' thereupon, hooked up a box fan through a quickly arranged duct and got to it. I had gotten well into making a pretty fair knife (about 4 2 hr days) when...

...the little old mexican lady from across the back fence showed up asking me to stop. Now mind you, I'm not complaining about that. I didn't want to be a nuisance so I had waited until 3:30 PM to get to work each day, and tbh that anvil rings a lot louder than I thought it would (which is fine by me from a strictly technical perspective).

She actually asked me to wait until 5:30 PM after which she said she'd be fine with it; it was while I was waiting this out that I read up on local noise ordinances, and well, I'm fucked if anyone ever complains to the local constabulary.

SO, I'm looking for a place to work. I have no formal training, other than some uncredited work in metallurgy with a college prof friend of mine, who helped me identify the metal in the leaf springs with scanning electron microscopy. The rest I'm pretty much making up as I go along.

I'll add pics of my smithy and the project later in the comments.

After making this post and reading on some of the other sites linked on this subverse, I was inspired to look around for local blacksmithing organizations, because in a place the size of Houston, there's bound to be a crowd of people doing just about anything worth doing.

Lo and behold, I found the folks at the Houston Area Blacksmith's Association (HABAIron). They hold classes/demos a couple times per month at the Armand Bayou Park, down on the east end of Bay Area Blvd. 20$/Yr for a membership, and members can come and use their forges and tools.

I'll be looking into it, if you're in my area you should too. They have a website at http://www.habairon.org/ and a Facebook page (if you're into that thing) at https://www.facebook.com/HoustonAreaBlacksmithsAssociationInc .

Stay tuned for the image dump :)

Cheers

Odd, because Texans are often the first to belittle California as being a nanny State, but I who live here in a suburban part of the Bay Area, can forge with impunity pretty much any time I want without fear of the police coming to tell me to stop, even if someone complains. I know this because I have complained several times to the local police force when my own neighbors have held parties and made really excessive noise, and been told by the police that there is nothing they can do about it. I have been forging here for almost 18 years now.

One thing you might consider is trying to make less noise when you forge. From what I have read, forklift tine is notorious for being very loud. You have a couple of anvil makers in Texas, Texas Farrier Supply and JHM anvils, both of which I believe cast anvils from ductile iron. I own a TFS 200 lb. anvil and find it to be very quiet compared to most others I have worked on. You can pick up a 150 lb. London Pattern anvil from them for $765.00 and although it would be a bit of a drive to get there from Houston, the savings on freight might make it worth while. You should be able to set one of these up so that there is essentially no ring at all.

If you follow my posts at all, you'll come to see I don't put much stock in what 'Texans' think vs what 'Californians' think vs. what 'viewers of South Park' think lol.

Just tell me what the man thinks and I'll have what I need to go on.

All that aside, thanks for the anvil maker info. I kinda like the way that fork rings, if I strike it just prior to the work, the anvil is still ringing when the hammer comes down, something I rather like as it is as if the anvil strikes from the bottom as I do from the top.

That being said, it may be a sacrifice I need to make in order to remain in play.

I've heard a number of methods for reducing anvil noise, but I'm not entirely sure if it would apply to you (I'm having trouble imagining what your setup looks like). I've heard you can wrap chains around the anvil and that they absorb some of the vibration (more mass = less noise). Personally I use heavy duty magnet on the side on my anvil when I'm working. Alternatively you could try and create a base between your "anvil" and anvil stand with caulking or rubber.

If you're looking for an upgrade for your anvil, one of buddies has a "City Anvil". Basically they are designed to reduce noise and absorb as much shock as possible, all within the anvil. Pricing obviously depends on the size you're looking for.

Hahaha, think of a one-note xylaphone and that's pretty much it. The section of forklift fork I'm using is the after half of the fork itself, the turn 'up' to where it hangs off the forklift, and about three inches of that vertical part, so I have a good 24" or so of flat working space, and the small raised portion on the turn of the fork, which I've ground most of the edges from giving me sort of table to fold things over.

It's very much cobbled together. That is something I really like about it, though I'm quite aware I'll likely end up out-growing it.

For now, it works great for what I'm doing (less the ringing problem).
